children.value: Show a photo of the Matterhorn to a current multimodal language model and ask for a description. The answer reads like the work of a careful human annotator: “The image centers on a single, dramatic mountain peak with a sharp, pyramid-like summit. Its steep faces are streaked with snow and dark gray rock. The peak looks like the Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps, a shape recognized around the world.” The model recognized a specific named entity, described the scene, the colors, and the lighting, and did so without any task-specific training.

applied them to sequences of image patches. Multimodal transformers combine both: they encode images, audio, or video together with text. For retrieval, they offer two paths across the semantic gap. The first path generates text that describes the content and then searches the text. The second path maps content and text into one shared embedding space and compares them directly. This section covers both and compares them.

has two parts. A visual encoder, usually a Vision Transformer, turns the image into a sequence of embeddings. A transformer decoder generates text token by token. Through cross-attention, each generated token looks at the image embeddings, so the words follow the visual content. Such models are trained on large collections of image-caption pairs. Current multimodal language models go one step further: the image embeddings enter a full language model together with a text prompt, so the user controls through the prompt what the model writes.
This control turns the model into a configurable metadata extractor.

shows a two-step pipeline for the Matterhorn photo. The first prompt asks for a detailed description of the main subject, the setting, the colors, and the lighting. The second prompt asks for a JSON document with predefined fields: a headline, keywords, named entities, dominant colors and shapes, extracted text, and boolean flags such as

Each field of the JSON document has a place in the index of

. The headline and the description become text fields for BM25 and for text embeddings. The keywords and named entities become fields for exact matching and facets. The boolean fields become filters: “outdoor photos without people” is a simple filter query. The prompt decides which metadata the archive gets, at which level, and in which format. Changing the schema means changing the prompt, not retraining a model. A good starting point for writing such prompts is to ask the model itself to draft a prompt from a short specification, a technique called meta-prompting.

The same path works for other media. A speech recognition model such as Whisper transcribes the spoken words of a podcast, an interview, or a video into text with timestamps. It is a transformer that encodes the audio signal and decodes text tokens, trained on 680,000 hours of weakly labeled audio from the web. Text recognition (OCR) extracts the words shown in images and videos, from street signs to presentation slides. For video, a multimodal model can describe the frames of each shot. In all cases, the output is text, and the complete text toolkit applies: BM25, embeddings, filters, and the retrieval-augmented generation of

The describe path has clear strengths. The metadata is readable, so an archivist can check and correct it. The search uses mature, cheap, and well-understood text indexes. Search results can be explained, because each hit matched specific words. But it also has a fundamental limit: the index contains only what the model chose to write at indexing time. If the description of a beach photo does not mention the red umbrella in the corner, the query “red umbrella” will not find the photo. Generating rich descriptions for every item is also expensive, because a large model must process each item once, and again whenever the prompt changes.

showed that classifiers confuse similar classes. Generated metadata adds an eighth obstacle that is harder to spot:

. A language model produces the most plausible continuation of its input, not a verified statement of fact. When the visual evidence is weak, it fills the gap with a plausible guess and states it with the same confidence as a correct observation. A mountain that resembles the Matterhorn may be labeled “Matterhorn”; a person in a suit at a lectern may be named after a well-known politician; text that is too small to read may be “extracted” anyway.

Hallucinations are especially harmful for specific metadata, such as names, places, and dates, because users trust exactly these fields. Several measures reduce the risk. The prompt can ask the model to mark uncertain values or to leave a field empty when the evidence is unclear. Generated values can be cross-checked against independent metadata: if the EXIF GPS coordinates place the photo in Canada, the label “Matterhorn” is wrong. Specific named entities can be restricted to a controlled list, such as the known persons of a news archive. For high-value collections, a human verifies the generated metadata, which is far cheaper than writing it from scratch.
Generated metadata looks better than it is

Generated descriptions are fluent, detailed, and consistent in style, so they look more reliable than the terse keywords of human annotators. It is tempting to judge the quality of generated metadata by reading a few examples. Evaluate it like any other classifier: sample items, compare the generated fields with ground truth, and measure precision and recall per field.
The second path avoids the detour through text.

(Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), published by OpenAI in 2021, trains two encoders side by side: a text encoder (a transformer) that maps a caption to a vector, and an image encoder (a Vision Transformer or a convolutional network) that maps an image to a vector of the same dimension. The training goal is that an image and its caption end up close together in this shared space.

The contrastive loss rewards high similarity on the diagonal and low similarity everywhere else: matching embeddings are pulled together, mismatched ones are pushed apart. No one labels classes; the captions that people wrote for their images on the web provide the supervision.

What if two captions fit the same image?

The diagonal rule is a simplification. If a batch contains two photos of snowy mountains, the caption of the second photo counts as a mismatch for the first, although it describes it well. The loss tolerates such collisions. It is a softmax over each row, so it only asks that the matching caption scores highest: once it leads by a few hundredths of cosine similarity, the push on the other caption practically stops, and both captions stay close to both photos. Such collisions are also rare in batches of 32,768 random pairs, and over many steps every mountain photo pulls its own mountain caption closer.
After training, the shared space supports retrieval in every direction. For

, the query is an image, and the same index returns visually and semantically similar images. For
, the system finds the captions or documents closest to an image.
The shared space also turns CLIP into a classifier for any set of classes, without training. For
, the system writes a short text prompt for each class, such as “a photo of a mountain”, encodes the prompts, and assigns the image to the class whose prompt is closest.

The same five prompts assign a photo of Roger Federer to “a photo of a tennis player” with 99.9998%: its similarity is 0.304, against 0.157 to 0.163 for the other prompts.

The absolute similarity values are low: even the best matches reach only 0.293 and 0.304. CLIP embeddings of images and texts occupy different regions of the shared space, so cross-modal cosine similarities typically fall between 0.1 and 0.4. What carries the information is the difference between the candidates, which the temperature amplifies. A threshold on the raw cosine, such as “relevant if above 0.5”, would reject every image.

Contrastive training is not limited to images. CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pre-training) applies the same idea to audio clips and their descriptions, so a query such as “dog barking in the rain” can retrieve sound recordings. Video models embed frames or short clips and align them with transcripts and captions. Newer models embed several modalities into one space.
The two paths answer different needs, and many systems use both.

The describe path excels at specific facts, filters, and explainable results: “photos of the Matterhorn taken in winter without people”. The embedding path excels at visual concepts that nobody thought to describe: “a lonely bench in the fog”. A hybrid system runs both and fuses the rankings with reciprocal rank fusion, as

does for sparse and dense text retrieval. The generated descriptions can also serve as passages in a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, where a language model answers questions about an image archive.
